opus-5.5.text:
I think stronger language understanding is valuable, but I'd be careful about how we frame it. For Physical AI, language isn't the core of the problem. Language is the interface.

Here's how I think about it. A physical AI system, whether it's a robot arm in a factory, a humanoid, or an autonomous vehicle, ultimately has to understand how the world works: geometry, contact, friction, cause and effect, what happens when you push something or when a pedestrian steps off the curb. That knowledge mostly isn't in text. You can read a million descriptions of how to fold a shirt and still not be able to fold one. So the foundation has to come from video, from sensor data, from simulation, from interaction. That's why we put so much effort into world foundation models. They learn the dynamics of the physical world from visual data.

Where language becomes really important is in three places.

First, specifying the task. Humans communicate intent through language. If I tell a robot "clear the table but leave the glasses," the model has to parse that, ground "glasses" to the right objects, and understand the implied constraint. The better the language understanding, the more naturally people can instruct these systems without engineering every task by hand.

Second, reasoning and planning. A lot of common-sense knowledge is encoded in language: kitchens have knives, knives are sharp, you hand them to someone handle first. Large language models absorbed a huge amount of this from text. Connecting that semantic knowledge to physical understanding lets the system handle long-horizon tasks and situations it hasn't seen. This is why we see value in reasoning models that can think through a physical scenario step by step before acting.

Third, data and supervision. Language is a great way to label and organize data at scale. If you can caption video richly and accurately, you can curate training data, describe edge cases, and generate synthetic scenarios from text prompts. Better language understanding directly improves the quality of the data pipeline.

So how do I judge its value? I ask: does the stronger language capability actually ground into better physical behavior? A model that can eloquently describe a scene but can't predict what happens next, or can't act on it, hasn't solved the problem. The benchmark should be whether the system follows instructions more reliably, generalizes to new tasks, and makes fewer physically wrong decisions, not whether it sounds smarter.

My view is that language and physics are complementary. Language gives you abstraction and the ability to communicate with humans. Physical world models give you grounding. The most capable systems will tightly integrate both, but if I had to say which one is the bottleneck today, it's still the physical understanding, not the language.

fable-5.1.text:
I think stronger language understanding matters a great deal, but maybe not for the reason people first assume. Language is not just an interface for giving a robot commands. It is the compressed record of how humans reason about the world. When we train a model on language, we are giving it access to all the common sense that humans have written down about causality, about intentions, about what happens when you drop a glass or push a door that is locked.

For Physical AI, that prior is incredibly valuable because physical data is expensive and scarce. A humanoid robot can only generate so many hours of real interaction. But if the model already understands, from language, that a cup of hot coffee should be carried carefully, that a child in the room means you should slow down, that "put this away" means something different in a kitchen than in a garage, then you need far fewer physical demonstrations to teach the actual motor skill. Language gives you a kind of scaffolding, so the physical learning can focus on the part that only physical experience can teach.

The second value is in task specification and generalization. If a robot can only understand a narrow vocabulary, you end up programming it task by task. With strong language understanding, you can describe a new task, decompose it into steps, handle exceptions in natural terms, and the robot can transfer what it knows. That is really what we mean by a generalist robot.

But I also want to be honest about the limit. Language understanding by itself does not give you physics. A model can describe perfectly what should happen when you pour water and still have no ability to pour water. Grounding is the hard part, meaning connecting those words to perception and to actions that actually work in the real world, with real friction and real latency. So I see language as a multiplier. If your physical foundation is weak, multiplying it by a strong language model does not help much. But once you have a decent world model and sensorimotor capability, language is what unlocks the scale and the flexibility. That is why we invest in both, and why the interesting research is at the intersection, where language, video and action are learned together rather than stitched afterward.

astra-6.text:
I would judge it by whether better language understanding leads to better actions in the physical world. Can the model understand what you want, connect that request to what it sees, and carry out the task reliably?

For example, if you ask a robot to clear a table, you are giving it a goal, not a detailed sequence of movements. The robot needs to interpret that goal in the context of the scene. And if the instruction is ambiguous, it needs to recognize that and ask for clarification.

So I would compare task success, how much human intervention is needed, and how well the system handles unfamiliar instructions and environments. Stronger language understanding is valuable if it improves those outcomes. Being able to explain a task fluently is useful, but the real test is whether the system can actually do it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the real test is whether stronger language understanding leads to better actions in the physical world. Can a robot understand your intent, connect that intent to what it sees, and act correctly—even when you haven’t specified every step?

For example, if you say, “Please clear the table,” there are many implicit decisions: what should be removed, what should stay, where things belong, and how to handle fragile objects. Language understanding can help interpret the goal, but the robot still needs perception, physical reasoning, and control to execute it.

So I would evaluate the value through task success, generalization to unfamiliar situations, and how much human guidance is required. If a model can explain an instruction beautifully but cannot carry it out reliably, the benefit for Physical AI is limited. The important thing is connecting understanding to action.
